body.text: In September 1941, at the height of the Second World War, British etcher, watercolourist and book illustrator Edward Julius Detmold exhibited his paintings for the last time at a little private gallery in the primly middle-class seaside town of Worthing. Detmold’s watercolours of birds and flowers were hung alongside those of other local artists, and the scant critical response to the exhibition was scathing. One local journalist summed up the works on display with the dismissive phrase “roses-round-the-cottage-door sentimentality.”

By the time the exhibition opened, Detmold himself — who was then in his late fifties — had retreated to the small Welsh town of Montgomery, where he was to spend the last decades of his life as a total recluse, hidden away in the rambling old house he shared with his mother, sister, brother-in-law and two male friends. In 1957 — impoverished, in poor health and going blind — he committed suicide, dying entirely forgotten by the art world. There were no memorials or obituaries. He is buried in an unmarked grave.

It was a sad end to the life of a man who had first exhibited at the Royal Academy at the age of thirteen, was acclaimed as a child genius, and went on to become one of the leading British book illustrators of the early twentieth century — the era known as the Golden Age of Illustration. There is also a particular irony in Detmold’s final exhibition. While the art that he was showing in public in his middle age consisted almost entirely of pretty but tritely conventional watercolours, in private he had been producing a searing set of paintings accompanied by a strange and visionary text, denouncing the violence of modern civilisation and hauntingly foreshadowing the horrors of the Second World War: a work that was never published or exhibited.

The contrasts between Detmold’s private imaginings and the tamely decorative art he showed to the public in the 1930s and 1940s are characteristic of this enigmatic man, who restlessly experimented with multiple artistic styles while resolutely hiding his personal life from prying eyes. These paradoxes also help to explain why assessments of his work have continued to be mixed, and why the few published studies of his life have been brief and marked by crucial lacunae.

I became aware of Detmold’s anti-war art during the Covid pandemic as I was setting out on a project to try to unravel the mysteries of the artist’s life. At the time, I thought of this project just as a little private quest — a distraction from the frustrations of Covid, which, at every turn, was blocking efforts to do more serious research. Edward Detmold and his family had been so successful in concealing the traces of his life that I assumed it would be impossible to discover enough to write a full biography; but gradually, unexpected doors opened, and a story began to emerge, almost like an image appearing from a photographic plate in an old-fashioned dark room. The more I saw, the more this story seemed to speak not just to the history of early twentieth-century art but also to profound concerns that continue to haunt us in the twenty-first century world.

I had first encountered Edward Detmold’s illustrations in my childhood, when my favourite of all books was a beautiful edition of the Arabian Nights owned by my mother. Although the text was in ponderous Victorian English and (to me) totally unreadable, the pictures seemed to draw me into a magical world of desert landscapes, enchanted palaces and hidden treasure chambers. The book’s cover, embossed with gold, bore in large letters the words “Illustrations by Detmold” — but no one could tell me who Detmold was. It was not until decades later, when I joined a group of colleagues writing essays about the books that had influenced us in childhood, that I started on a quest for Detmold which has lasted for more than twenty-five years.

The more I discovered, the more mystifying the story seemed to become. The illustrator of the Arabian Nights, Edward Julius Detmold, was one of a pair of twins descended from an eminent German Jewish family. Their grandfather had migrated to Britain, and they were born in suburban London in 1883, but their upbringing and that of their sister was supervised by an enigmatic guardian sometimes described as their uncle (which he wasn’t).

Both boys showed prodigious talents as artists from an early age. They were mentored and encouraged by the famous pre-Raphaelite Edward Burne Jones and published their first illustrated book when they were just fifteen, later going on to produce a famous set of illustrations for Rudyard Kipling’s Jungle Book and to win acclaim for their exquisite etchings of the natural world. But then in 1908, at the height of their success, and for reasons which have never properly been explained, Edward’s twin, Charles Maurice Detmold, committed suicide.

Edward responded by throwing himself more passionately than ever into his art. Between 1908 and the mid 1920s, he created a series of illustrations for books including Aesop’s Fables, the works of naturalists Jean Henri Fabre and William Henry Hudson, and anthologies by Nobel Prize–winning author Maurice Maeterlinck. He also worked with the children’s writer Florence Dugdale and the man who was soon to be her husband, novelist Thomas Hardy, on a series of children’s picture books about birds and beasts which were part of the emerging British animal protection movement. (Hardy, who contributed to the books anonymously, was a central figure in this movement).

In the 1920s Detmold returned to etching, which he had abandoned shortly before the suicide of his twin. The most popularly successful of his wide-ranging experiments in this medium were his images of imagined desert scenes: the scenes he also painted so vividly in his last and most famous illustrated work, the Arabian Nights, published in 1924.

But it emerged that another source of trauma, unnoticed by those who have written about the artist’s life, had shaped Edward Detmold’s vision of the world. His lifelong aversion to violence led him, in 1916, to refuse to fight in the First World War. He was hauled before a magistrate’s court, where his plea to be recognised as a conscientious objector on moral grounds received short shrift. The magistrate’s blunt response was “I have nothing to do with morality in this court.” Detmold was forcibly enrolled in an army training unit and, when he refused to obey orders, was court martialled and briefly imprisoned before being sent to one of the gruelling Home Office work camps set up to discipline conscientious objectors.

He never wrote, and barely seems to have spoken about, this experience, but its shadow is palpable in his 1930s anti-war art and in three little mystical texts he published in the early 1920s. These works appear to be influenced by Buddhist ideas, though Detmold never directly cites the Buddhist classics, nor, indeed, the work of any other writers. His spiritual writings express a passionate rejection of materialism and seek to map out a quietist path of self-reformation in order to overcome the greed and violence of the modern world: “we are reaping chaos, for we have followed the ways of disorder; there is no hope at all for us, but that we change our ways.”

After Edward Detmold’s death in 1957, his paintings and other possessions remained in the house in Montgomery where he had spent his final years. Then, one by one, the other members of the household also died. Detmold’s sister Nora was the last survivor — living on into her nineties, alone and largely bedridden as the empty house crumbled around her. When neighbours and strangers entered the building after her death in 1976, they found some 1500 drawings and paintings — most by Edward but some by Charles and other artists — jumbled in mountains of confusion among books, personal papers and other memorabilia.

Everything was inherited by the brother of one of Detmold’s lifelong companions — an elderly man who apparently had little interest in art. The paintings and etchings were sent to auction and the remaining contents of the house thrown out or burnt. Nothing was left to shed light on Edward Detmold’s private thoughts or personality — no letters, no diaries, no family photographs. Or so it seemed.

But in fact, two things had survived almost unnoticed. One was a cache of letters exchanged between Detmold and the publisher Joseph Malaby Dent, whose company — J.M. Dent and Sons — had published some of Detmold’s nature illustrations as well as his mystical texts. As these reveal, it was Dent who had rescued Detmold from the miseries of the First World War labour camp. Somehow, in 1918, the publisher managed to persuade the authorities to release him from custody to work for him (under strict supervision) throughout the final months of the war.

Detmold’s letters to Dent give a vivid sense of the artist’s state of mind as he returned to freedom. After J.M. Dent and Sons was sold to Weidenfeld & Nicolson in 1986, the company’s archive ended up in the library of the University of North Carolina. There, tucked away in a file, are Detmold’s letters, written in his small and tidy handwriting, expressing his joy at being able once again to immerse himself in the natural world he loved:

I am working as long as daylight will allow, in the hope of letting you have two complete drawings next Saturday morning between 10.30 and 12, “The Nightingale” and the apple drawings… I am having every opportunity of studying the nightingale. He is now singing night and day quite close at hand. Four young robins are just hatched out in the garden.

It was not all plain sailing, though. There were constant criticisms from naturalists who wanted illustrations of birds and animals to be meticulously scientific. Edward Detmold’s work, by contrast, was a pre-Raphaelite-inspired reinterpretation of the natural world, expressing his sense of identification with the lives even of the smallest creatures. As he wrote to Dent, in response to some of his critics:

I can never look at the wondrous living things without being moved. I cannot regard them in cold blood as certain colours and forms of certain dimensions — as so many do who are better fitted than myself for this diagram function… It is not the cold-blooded expert who labels things, but the big-hearted lover of all living things that I hope to appeal to.

A more surprising piece of serendipity led to the rescue of another archival fragment that opens an unexpected window into Edward Detmold’s world. When the contents of the Detmolds’ house were being thrown out after Nora’s death, a neighbour noticed a rather nice wooden box in one of the dustbins and, thinking that it might come in handy, fished it out. The box turned out to contain 42 glass plate photographic negatives that eventually made their way into the collection of Montgomery’s Old Bell Museum. One photo in the box was the portrait of Edward Detmold reproduced above, but the others remained unlabelled and unidentified for nearly fifty years. Putting them together with the letters to J.M. Dent, the landscape of Detmold’s life comes into new focus.

At the time when he was working for Dent, Edward Detmold was spending much of his time in a country cottage owned by his mother, outside the little Sussex town of Steyning. The photos — almost all of which are of animals or of the rolling Sussex downland — match the countryside around Steyning, and we can tell that some at least were taken by Detmold because they include an image which he used as the basis for one of his early book illustrations.

Like his paintings and etchings, the photos express Detmold’s absorption in the world of nature. Where (rarely) human beings appear in the images, they are almost always overshadowed by the presence of the animals who accompany them. Other photographs reveal the profound influence of Asian art on the Detmold twins’ work: interior shots of their cottage show walls covered with East Asian prints and screens, and shelves lined with Japanese and Chinese porcelain.

There is so much that remains a mystery. One of the photos in the Detmold collection shows a strange and haunting image of a man — dressed in Indian garb and posing as a snake charmer — gazing into the eyes of a (presumably artificial) serpent wrapped around his arm. Is this the only known photo of Edward Detmold’s twin Charles Maurice, taken shortly before his suicide? Circumstantial evidence suggests that it is, but we will probably never know for sure.

Although hardly anyone I spoke to about the project recognised the name of the artist whose life I was researching, a surprising number recognised the Detmolds’ illustrations when they saw them. The visual images we see in childhood remain imprinted on the brain long after we have forgotten the words and names that go with them.

We are like Neela, the main character of Pradeep Sebastian’s “bibliomystery” The Book Hunters of Katpadi (Hachette India, 2017), who forgets the title of the favourite children’s book that she is seeking — “in the sad way we do with most things from our childhood” — but has never forgotten the illustrations: “All I can remember is that there were these extraordinary pictures of wild animals — they were lifelike, detailed and yet with mythical qualities to them.” It is an elderly antiquarian book expert who, in one of the novel’s pivotal scenes, recognises her description. When Neela asks him if he knows the book, he instantly replies, “I know the illustrator — E. J. Detmold.”

I hope my new book, Nature, War and the Art of the Detmold Twins, not only puts a name to the images but also helps readers to learn more of the strange but intriguing personality behind the name. Despite Edward Detmold’s reclusive individualism and the fanciful nostalgia of some of his later paintings, the delicate power of his finest nature etchings and illustrations continues to enchant and inspire. At times, his work echoes the simple stereotypes of Orientalism, while his mystical writings have sometimes been dismissed (too casually, I think) as the wanderings of an unstable mind. Yet, as curator and art critic Rodney Engen writes, the Detmold twins’ “superb prints, book illustrations and paintings remain unrivalled depictions of an almost surreal approach to nature.”

In an age of climate change, species extinction, and rising global military tensions, Edward Detmold’s paintings and etchings, together with the works of his lost twin, still speak to us. They invite us to look deeply and immersively at the natural world around us, and to confront — within ourselves and within our society — the origins of the violence that threatens to destroy it. As Edward Detmold wrote in the wake of the First World War, in words that still resonate today: “we ourselves are the constituents of our world, and we are men and women, not clay moulded from without… our world is given into our power, what shall we make of it for ourselves and one another?” •
Tessa Morris-Suzuki’s Nature, War and the Art of the Detmold Twins is published by Routledge.
